**This is a pre-release for testing.** It is not marked Latest and is not intended for general use. If you want a stable build, use v0.4.6.

Linux x86_64 only — this pre-release ships the tarball. No `.deb`, `.rpm` or AUR package is built for previews.

This is the **last alpha**. The line moves to beta next, so this is the build we most want flown.

---

## The headline: long flights should use substantially less memory

Two changes, both aimed at issue #227 — the OOM kill that ended a 12-hour flight at 64 GB.

**Tiles are no longer copied to be served.** A generated texture is 11.17 MiB and X-Plane reads about 4% of it, in two calls. Delivering it used to copy the whole thing — out of the cache, again through each of two coalescers, again on the job result, once more per reply — even when the bytes were already resident. The payload is now reference-counted end to end.

**Tiles are now returned to the operating system when freed.** This one is subtle and was the bigger term. glibc serves an 11 MiB allocation either by `mmap`, which gives the memory back on free, or from an internal arena, which does not. Its threshold for choosing *adapts upward* every time a large block is freed, and passes 11 MiB after a single tile. From that point every arena that ever served a tile keeps that space for the life of the process — and glibc allows up to eight arenas per CPU core.

### Measured

A 4.3-hour flight against a same-build flight on default settings, compared at **matched work** rather than matched time:

| tiles generated | before | after | |
|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 10,000 | 8,954 MB | 6,956 MB | 22% less |
| 20,000 | 11,143 MB | 7,003 MB | 37% less |
| 39,157 | 13,721 MB | 8,970 MB | **35% less** |

### What we are *not* claiming

**This does not close #227.** The flight ended at 39,157 tiles; the comparison flight gained a further 5.9 GB beyond that point, and we have not tested past it. What is established is that the steep early retention is bounded. **A long haul — six hours or more — is the single most useful thing you can fly on this build.**

## Reading the memory trace

The `Memory sample` line (every 60 seconds, INFO level) gained five fields. If you report memory behaviour, these are the ones that matter.

### Quote `anon_mb + swap_mb`. Do not quote `vm_mb`.

`anon_mb + swap_mb` is the **committed footprint** — the memory the process actually holds, and what the OOM killer scores. It is also what your system monitor shows.

`vm_mb` is address space, which includes mappings that are reserved but never touched. Thread stacks alone measure 2.21 MB each, against a worker pool that cycles between 37 and 586 threads — so `vm_mb` carries a **sawtooth of roughly a gigabyte that is not memory at all**. Two of us reading this trace mistook that artifact for a real finding before it was identified. It will mislead you too.

### The allocator fields

| observation | meaning |
|---|---|
| `heap_free_mb` rising | the allocator is holding free space it has not returned |
| `inuse_mb` rising | the process genuinely holds more objects |
| `mmap_mb` falling while `heap_mb` rises | the threshold fix has stopped working — worth reporting |
| all four flat while `anon_mb` climbs | growth is somewhere other than the allocator |

At shutdown a `malloc_trim at shutdown` line reports how much of the footprint was releasable.

### A healthy line looks like this

```
Memory sample uptime_s=15600 rss_mb=8823 vm_mb=11252 swap_mb=54 anon_mb=8916
  threads=70 heap_mb=3542 mmap_mb=5406 inuse_mb=859 heap_free_mb=2683
  tiles_done=39157 chunks_ok=10023424 chunks_failed=0
  fuse_dds_reads=... fuse_dds_read_mb=4710 fuse_dds_alloc_mb=4710
  dds_handles_peak=32 dds_pinned_peak_mb=181 dds_budget_exhausted=0
```

Points of reference from an 11.5-hour flight: `heap_mb` reached a ceiling and stopped growing after about two hours; `fuse_dds_alloc_mb` equalled `fuse_dds_read_mb` at every sample; `dds_budget_exhausted` stayed at 0.

**Counters are cumulative since start.** Nothing resets them, so a raw value always climbs — difference two samples to get a rate. `regions_deferred` climbing is not a fault.

## Also in this release

**Arch and CachyOS packages build again** (#222). The release workflow was re-authoring the PKGBUILD rather than using the one in the repository, and its copy omitted the flag that disables link-time optimisation — which Arch enables by default, and which caused linking to fail with every symbol of one dependency undefined. Reported by @goon818. The release job now builds the package before shipping it, so this class of breakage cannot reach a release again.

**Handle budget exhaustion is now visible** (#236). Past its ceiling, the per-open tile cache silently stopped memoising and reads got slower with no symptom. It is now counted and warned once.

**Counter semantics corrected** (#229). Several counters were documented as per-interval and were in fact cumulative. The documentation now matches the code.

---

## How to report

The log is at `~/.xearthlayer/xearthlayer.log` and **is overwritten on every launch** — copy it aside before relaunching or it is gone.

Most useful report:

1. Route and duration, and whether the cache was cold
2. The **first and last** `Memory sample` lines
3. `anon_mb + swap_mb` at the start and end, and `tiles_done` at the end
4. Anything visually wrong — misaligned, black or corrupted ground textures are serious, because these changes alter which bytes get served

Please do **not** set `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` or `MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_` unless you are deliberately running an allocator experiment — the build now sets the threshold itself, and an environment override silently replaces it. If you do set one, say so, since the log records it.
